record.paper_title: Ultra-Dense Cell-Free Massive MIMO for 6G: Technical Overview and Open Questions
record.original_question: Under what propagation, density, antenna, processing, and traffic conditions is the channel-hardening or use-and-then-forget bounding technique a reliable achievable-rate tool for cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO), and when should researchers instead use full-side-information bounds with downlink training, blind channel estimation, non-coherent bounds, enhanced normalized precoding, or scheduling changes?

evidence.quote: D. When Does the Hardening Bounding Technique Work?

In CF-MMIMO, since only a subset of APs serves a given user and the channels from different APs have different large-scale fading coefficients, the level of channel hardening may not be as pronounced.
In some practical scenarios, particularly in UDNs, channels from a given user to different APs may not be independent, and hence, the channel hardening is not guaranteed.
In these scenarios, more suitable bounding techniques become necessary and the associated channel acquisition schemes should be considered.

In some practical systems, especially with bursty traffic where the users have dynamic buffers, the user scheduling is done every transmission time interval (TTI) and over narrow frequency bands. Consequently, the set of active users changes quickly over time/frequency. In such cases, this bound may not be the most suitable approach.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) wireless system consisting of a large number of geographically distributed access points (APs), each equipped with one or more antennas, jointly serving a set of single-antenna user equipments (UEs) over a shared time-frequency resource. The channel from UE k to AP m is modeled as a random vector h_{mk} whose distribution depends on a large-scale fading coefficient β_{mk} (capturing path loss and shadowing) and a small-scale fading component (e.g., Rayleigh, Rician, or correlated complex Gaussian). Each UE is served by a (possibly user-specific) subset M_k of APs. Channel state information is obtained at the APs by uplink pilot transmission and (potentially) further refined by downlink pilots, blind estimation, or non-coherent schemes. Linear precoders/combiners (such as maximum-ratio, zero-forcing, or MMSE) are applied at the APs, and per-user achievable downlink and uplink rates are evaluated.

A classical analytical tool, called the "use-and-then-forget" (UatF) or hardening bound, lower-bounds the ergodic achievable rate of UE k by treating the effective channel mean as a deterministic known coefficient and lumping all deviations from it into a Gaussian-noise interference term. This bound is tight when the effective channel exhibits channel hardening, i.e., when |h_eff,k|^2 concentrates sharply around its mean E[|h_eff,k|^2].

Problem. Characterize, rigorously and quantitatively, the regimes—specified in terms of (i) propagation conditions (line-of-sight vs. NLOS, spatial correlation, channel-vector independence across APs), (ii) AP/UE density and geometry, (iii) per-AP antenna numbers and array configuration, (iv) signal-processing choices (precoder family, normalization, pilot allocation, power control), and (v) traffic and scheduling assumptions—under which the UatF/hardening lower bound is a reliable (asymptotically tight) achievable-rate tool for CF-MMIMO. Conversely, determine for which of these regimes the UatF bound becomes loose, and identify which alternative achievable-rate techniques—full-CSI / genie-aided bounds, bounds incorporating downlink pilot training, blind channel estimation–based bounds, non-coherent capacity bounds, enhanced normalized precoding schemes, or modified user scheduling—yield provably tighter achievable rates. Provide quantitative thresholds (e.g., on the variance-to-mean-squared ratio of the effective channel gain) separating these regimes.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction concerning when the use-and-then-forget / hardening lower bound is reliable in cell-free massive MIMO and what bounding techniques should replace it in ultra-dense regimes. Recent literature on CF-MMIMO continues to develop alternative rate bounds (genie-aided, downlink-pilot-aided, non-coherent), but a comprehensive, quantitative characterization across propagation, density, antenna, processing, and traffic regimes has not been established, so the problem is best classified as open.

status_evidence.title: Ultra-Dense Cell-Free Massive MIMO for 6G: Technical Overview and Open Questions
status_evidence.snippet: Survey identifying open questions including when the hardening bounding technique is valid in CF-MMIMO.
status_evidence.claim: The validity regime of the hardening bound and choice of alternative bounds is listed as an open problem.
